purpose: Machine-readable receipt for the measurement LLP 0168 and LLP 0169 rest on: a plain-HTTP non-localhost origin loses Web Locks, and therefore loses the browser persistence arm, while the identical app on localhost keeps it.

method.probe: Runtime.evaluate over CDP against the running Expo web bundle
method.cors: curl with an explicit Origin header against the Snapback dev server
method.controls: Same machine, same app bundle, same backend, same moment. Only the page origin differs between the two rows.

browserContext.note: Terminal memory fallback. IndexedDB is present and unused: the browser arm requires Web Locks as well.
Same bundle, same backend. localhost is a secure context, so Web Locks is defined and the browser arm engages.

conclusions: The two failures are independent. CORS blocks the request (loud, app refuses to boot). The secure-context loss degrades persistence to memory (silent).
The persistence degradation is NOT caused by IndexedDB being unavailable; IndexedDB is present in both rows. It is caused by navigator.locks being undefined outside a secure context.
Fixing CORS alone would therefore make the silent failure MORE likely, by removing the error that currently prevents booting.
honestCaveats: The localhost row's page also showed SNAPBACK_REACT_BINDING_MISMATCH at capture time, because codegen had been regenerated after the dev server loaded its artifacts. That is a developmentSync condition unrelated to the store facts: rqsStoreInfo is resolved by the client at construction, before binding admission, and the store implementation reported is therefore unaffected.
This receipt is a local-target dev measurement on one machine and one Chrome version. It is evidence for the causal chain, not a cross-browser or cross-platform claim.
Safari and Firefox were not measured. Web Locks secure-context gating is specified behavior, not Chrome-specific, but that is inference here rather than measurement.
